qAndA.answer: The narrator selects the "AutoCAD ISO" template.
qAndA.question: What template does the narrator choose for the new AutoCAD file?

qAndA.answer: The narrator uses the dimension tool to measure the length indicated on the provided scale within the image.
qAndA.question: How does the narrator measure the scale in the imported image?

qAndA.answer: The narrator reduces the contrast to make the image lines less bright and improve the visibility of the cursor and future linework.
qAndA.question: Why does the narrator adjust the image contrast?

qAndA.answer: The line serves as a reference for scaling the image. The narrator aims to make the scale in the image match the length of this reference line.
qAndA.question: What is the purpose of the 5-meter long line the narrator draws?

qAndA.answer: The narrator uses the "Scale by Reference" function, selecting a point on the image scale and the corresponding point on the 5-meter reference line. This scales the entire image proportionally.
qAndA.question: How does the narrator ensure the image is scaled accurately?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: In this tutorial I will show you how to import a raster image into AutoCAD and then
scale it so that you can begin to trace over the image and create vector line
work based on a raster image. You can start by opening on a new file. From the
templates I'll choose the A CAD ISO. This should automatically open a blank file
which has the units preset to millimeters. I can double check that by clicking
on the AutoCAD icon in the upper left corner and then going down to drawing
utilities and units. And here we can see our units are set to millimeters.
Everything else looks fine as well. Let's say okay. So I'm going to start off by
importing my raster image. Click on the insert tab to the top and then go to
attach. And then this will ask me to basically navigate to my to my image. Once
you find your image you'll get this dialog box which has a few options. In
this pane you have a preview of your image. Under Path type you have a few
options either full path or relative path or no path. In search and point we
can check this and then we can place it wherever we want. We leave it unchecked.
It would just place it at the origin 0 0 0. Which is fine. Scale. We don't need to
adjust because we would do that once we import the image. Rotation should be
fine as well. So we'll just say okay. And then if we zoom out we can see the
image here at our origin. The other way we could have imported that is by
typing x-ref and hitting enter. And then we get this dialog box. And if you
click on this, I told them next to the twg icon which allows you to change to
attach image and a few other options as well. So if we attach image we basically
get the same options of navigating towards our image. So now we have our image.
The first problem is it's quite bright. I can barely see my cursor over top of
it. So to fix that I'm going to select the image and AutoCAD automatically
switches to the image tab where I can adjust this fader. Basically turn down
the contrast in this image allowing me to see my cursor and line work on top of
it much easier. So next we will try to figure out how big this image is. We can use
this scale here in the bottom of the image. We can go ahead and measure it.
typing distance. Click one end of the scale and then click near the other end of
the scale. And that says 69.2 millimeters. So that is very small in comparison to
what we actually want which is 5 millimeters or 5,000 millimeters. So rather than
doing the math and multiplying this image by a specific number we can scale
by reference. So what I would do first is create a line of reference. Basically a
line that's 5,000 millimeters long or 5 meters long which is what I want this
part of the image to be when it's all scaled accurately. So I will get as
close to I can to one end of the scale in the image. Then I will draw a line
that is 5 meters long or 5,000 millimeters. If I zoom out I enter to complete
command. You can see this line represents actually 5 meters. So next all we
have to do is scale up this image so that the scale in the image matches the
5 meter long line. So I will select the image and then go back to my home tab at
the top. In the modify tools you'll find scale. If I click on that down at the
bottom here it's asking me to select my object and I want to scale my image. So I
will select the image and hit enter and now the bottom it's asking the bottom
it's asking me to specify a base point. That's basically the point around which I
want to scale the object. So I will use the starting point of my line and which
is also the starting point of the scale in the image. Now I'll click there once and
now it's saying specify specify scale factor and then in parentheses it says copy or reference.
In those brackets those are my two additional options. I can choose to scale this as a copy
which I do not want to do this time or I can scale it with reference which is what I want.
So in order to activate one or the other of those commands I could type C for copy or
R for reference. So I will type R for reference and hit enter. Now it's asking me for reference
length. My reference length is the length of the scale in the drawing. First I will click
on end of my scale which is also the base point of my whole scaling operation. Now it's
asking for the reference length which is the length of the scale in the raster image.
So I will get as close as I can to the other end of this scale and click a second time.
Now you'll see it's asking for a new length and the new length is the length of my 5 meter long line.
So I will snap to the end of that line and now as you can see my 5 meter long line and my 5 meter scale in the image are exactly the same.
And from here I can set up a few layers and then begin to trace over this image and recreate this as an AutoCAD drawing.

youtube_description:
How to reference a raster image and then scale it to be 1:1.  This allows you to trace over the image and recreate the raster image as an AutoCAD dwg.

The image used in this example is of MVRDV's Plot 12 House in Borneo Sporenburg.

AutoCAD 2012 was used here.
youtube_title: AutoCAD - Import Raster Image & Scale for Tracing (AUTOCAD 2012)
